Neonates of the Great fruit-eating bat Artibeus lituratus are altricial at live birth, weighing an average of 10.5 grams [Wwb = 10.5 grams]. This modest neonatal mass is typical for a frugivorous phyllostomid and represents a small fraction of the adult female body size. Under the stable thermal conditions of the Neotropical roosts they inhabit, generally around 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the postpartum development follows a rapid trajectory. The gestation period, for instance, lasts 106 days [tg = 106 days], a duration that is comparatively extended within the genus and may reflect the energetic demands of sustaining foetal development while the mother maintains a high-fruit diet at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. Following parturition, the newborn undergoes a period of intense maternal investment during which it remains permanently attached to the teat for the first several weeks of life. This altricial strategy imposes significant metabolic costs on the lactating female.

This estimate, which is based on comparative data from the congener Artibeus watsoni, indicates a relatively short period of exclusive lactation for a bat of this size. During this nursing stage, the female must sustain her own basal metabolic requirements while also provisioning the growing offspring. The peak basal metabolic rate measured for this species is 84.80 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 84.80 milliliters of oxygen per hour], recorded at an ambient temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] which approximates the thermoneutral zone for this bat. This metabolic rate is notably high and likely supports the energetic costs of flight and lactation. The suckling juvenile thus depends entirely on its mother's ability to maintain a positive energy balance during this critical developmental window.

Sexual maturation in the Great fruit-eating bat is a relatively delayed process compared to other small mammals, with individuals typically reaching puberty at 288 days after birth [tp = 288 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This developmental milestone, occurring under the same thermoneutral conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], marks the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation. Females attain a definitive adult body mass of 70.1 grams [Wwi = 70.1 grams], a figure that represents the ultimate wet weight for adult females in this species, while some databases report a slightly lower average of 65.9 grams for general adult weight. This mass is consistent with the species' status as one of the larger members of its genus. The prolonged juvenile phase, spanning nearly ten months from birth to puberty, allows for the complete development of the skeletal and muscular systems necessary for sustained flight and foraging efficiency in a competitive frugivore guild.

Female Artibeus lituratus exhibit a seasonally constrained reproductive schedule that maximizes offspring survival within the predictable fruiting cycles of their habitat. Field observations indicate that females produce two litters per year of a single pup each [Ri = two litters per year of a single pup each], a reproductive frequency that occurs under the thermal regime of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] and balances the high energetic costs of gestation and lactation against the availability of fruit resources. The single-pup litter is characteristic of many phyllostomid bats and reflects a life-history strategy favoring offspring quality over quantity, as each newborn receives intensive maternal care and a high-quality milk supply. The timing of births is closely synchronized with periods of peak fruit abundance, ensuring that weaning coincides with maximum food availability for the juvenile.

Longevity data for Artibeus lituratus suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 3980 days [am = approximately 3980 days] when maintained under the stable conditions of their natural environment at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable among Neotropical bats and is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, low annual fecundity, and high adult survival rates. The species' ability to reach such an advanced age is likely facilitated by its frugivorous diet, which provides a reliable and nutritionally adequate food source year-round in many parts of its range. Additionally, the use of stable, predator-protected roost sites in tree cavities or foliage tents reduces extrinsic mortality risks. The interplay between this long reproductive window and the modest annual reproductive output of two pups per year underscores a conservative, K-selected demographic profile.
